claim: Most cortical neurons fire regularly when excited by a constant stimulus.
source: Most cortical neurons fire regularly when excited by a constant stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract to contrast with irregular-spiking neurons.

claim: Irregular-spiking (IS) interneurons are remarkable for the intrinsic variability of their spike timing.
source: In contrast, irregular-spiking (IS) interneurons are remarkable for the intrinsic variability of their spike timing, which can synchronize amongst IS cells via specific gap junctions.
evidence: This is a characterizing statement about IS interneurons supported by the experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: IS cells can synchronize amongst themselves via specific gap junctions.
source: In contrast, irregular-spiking (IS) interneurons are remarkable for the intrinsic variability of their spike timing, which can synchronize amongst IS cells via specific gap junctions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling results in Figure 7c,d.

claim: Spike time irregularity in IS cells is generated by a nonlinear dynamical interaction of voltage-dependent sodium and fast-inactivating potassium channels just below spike threshold.
source: Using patch-clamp recordings, artificial dynamic conductance injection, pharmacological analysis and computational modeling, we show that spike time irregularity is generated by a nonlinear dynamical interaction of voltage-dependent sodium and fast-inactivating potassium channels just below spike threshold, amplifying channel noise.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figures 3-5 and modeling in Figures 6-7.

claim: The nonlinear dynamical interaction of voltage-dependent channels amplifies channel noise.
source: Using patch-clamp recordings, artificial dynamic conductance injection, pharmacological analysis and computational modeling, we show that spike time irregularity is generated by a nonlinear dynamical interaction of voltage-dependent sodium and fast-inactivating potassium channels just below spike threshold, amplifying channel noise.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling in Figure 6d showing that both stochastic gKt and voltage-gated sodium conductance are required for large subthreshold fluctuations.

claim: Active irregularity may help IS cells synchronize with each other at gamma range frequencies.
source: This active irregularity may help IS cells synchronize with each other at gamma range frequencies, while resisting synchronization to lower input frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 8 showing differential synchronization at 10 Hz vs 40 Hz.

claim: IS cells resist synchronization to lower input frequencies.
source: This active irregularity may help IS cells synchronize with each other at gamma range frequencies, while resisting synchronization to lower input frequencies.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 8 showing reduced synchronization at 10 Hz compared to 40 Hz.

claim: Irregularity of firing in neurons can arise because of fluctuating patterns of synaptic input due to spontaneous activity.
source: Irregularity of firing in neurons can arise because of fluctuating patterns of synaptic input due to spontaneous activity (Destexhe et al., 2001), or from stochastic fluctuations in the release of transmitter (Ribrault et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature as a known mechanism of irregularity.

claim: Irregularity of firing in neurons can arise from stochastic fluctuations in the release of transmitter.
source: Irregularity of firing in neurons can arise because of fluctuating patterns of synaptic input due to spontaneous activity (Destexhe et al., 2001), or from stochastic fluctuations in the release of transmitter (Ribrault et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature as a known mechanism of irregularity.

claim: Certain types of neurons show strikingly high irregularity of firing even when isolated in vitro.
source: In some regions of the brain, though, certain types of neuron show strikingly high irregularity of firing even when isolated in vitro (Cauli et al., 1997; Grace and Bunney, 1984; Ascoli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and confirmed by the authors' own observations in Figure 1.

claim: The cellular mechanisms of intrinsic irregularity are unknown.
source: The cellular mechanisms of such intrinsic irregularity are unknown, though the stochastic gating of the ion channels involved in spike generation seems likely to play a part.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Stochastic gating of ion channels involved in spike generation seems likely to play a part in intrinsic irregularity.
source: The cellular mechanisms of such intrinsic irregularity are unknown, though the stochastic gating of the ion channels involved in spike generation seems likely to play a part.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated before the study's findings, which is then confirmed by the experimental results.

claim: Effective chaos in the nonlinear dynamics of voltage-dependent ion channels could contribute to irregular patterns of membrane potential.
source: Effective chaos in the nonlinear dynamics of the voltage-dependent ion channels involved in spike generation could also contribute to irregular patterns of membrane potential (Durstewitz and Gabriel, 2007; Fan and Chay, 1994).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature as a potential mechanism.

claim: The fast-spiking (FS, parvalbumin-expressing, basket morphology) cell network has a crucial role in the emergence of the gamma rhythm.
source: For example, the fast-spiking (FS, parvalbumin-expressing, basket morphology) cell network has a crucial role in the emergence of the gamma rhythm (Cardin et al., 2009; Hasenstaub et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature as established knowledge about FS cells.

claim: Recent evidence suggests the possibility of a specific role for the low-threshold-spiking (LTS, somatostatin-positive, Martinotti) cell network in lower frequency theta or beta rhythms.
source: Recent evidence suggests the possibility of a similar specific role for the low-threshold-spiking (LTS, somatostatin-positive, Martinotti) cell network in lower frequency theta or beta rhythms (Fanselow et al., 2008; Vierling-Claassen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from recent literature as emerging evidence.

claim: Irregular-spiking (IS) neurons are distinguished by their intrinsically irregular repetitive firing.
source: One type of interneuron, however, is distinguished by its intrinsically irregular repetitive firing, showing a broad, apparently random dispersion of its interspike intervals, as opposed to bursting, even when pharmacologically disconnected from any synaptic input.
evidence: This is a characterizing statement supported by experimental observations in Figure 1.

claim: IS neurons show a broad, apparently random dispersion of their interspike intervals.
source: One type of interneuron, however, is distinguished by its intrinsically irregular repetitive firing, showing a broad, apparently random dispersion of its interspike intervals, as opposed to bursting, even when pharmacologically disconnected from any synaptic input.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1d showing the ISI distribution.

claim: IS neurons maintain irregular firing even when pharmacologically disconnected from any synaptic input.
source: One type of interneuron, however, is distinguished by its intrinsically irregular repetitive firing, showing a broad, apparently random dispersion of its interspike intervals, as opposed to bursting, even when pharmacologically disconnected from any synaptic input.
evidence: This is stated in the text and confirmed by experiments performed in the presence of synaptic blockers.

claim: A mouse line with green fluorescent protein (GFP) linked to the promoter for Gad2 (GAD65) was used to enable specific targeting of IS cells.
source: To enable specific targeting of IS cells, we used a mouse line with green fluorescent protein (GFP) linked to the promoter for Gad2 (GAD65; López-Bendito et al., 2004), in which fluorescently labeled neurons in somatosensory cortex predominantly have an IS phenotype (Galarreta et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the experimental model used in the study.

claim: Fluorescently labeled neurons in somatosensory cortex of Gad2-GFP mice predominantly have an IS phenotype.
source: To enable specific targeting of IS cells, we used a mouse line with green fluorescent protein (GFP) linked to the promoter for Gad2 (GAD65; López-Bendito et al., 2004), in which fluorescently labeled neurons in somatosensory cortex predominantly have an IS phenotype (Galarreta et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and confirmed by the authors' observations.

claim: IS cells express CCK, VIP and 5HT3a receptors.
source: These cells express CCK, VIP and 5HT3a receptors (Sugino et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature characterizing these cells.

claim: IS cells are concentrated in layer 2.
source: They are concentrated in layer 2 (López-Bendito et al., 2004), and derive primarily from the caudal ganglionic eminence during development (López-Bendito et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and confirmed by the authors' observations in Figure 1a.

claim: IS cells derive primarily from the caudal ganglionic eminence during development.
source: They are concentrated in layer 2 (López-Bendito et al., 2004), and derive primarily from the caudal ganglionic eminence during development (López-Bendito et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature on the developmental origin of these cells.

claim: IS cells connect specifically to each other by gap junctions and mutually inhibitory synaptic connections.
source: They connect specifically to each other by gap junctions and mutually inhibitory synaptic connections, which together enable precisely-synchronized irregular firing (Galarreta et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature on the connectivity of these cells.

claim: Gap junctions and mutually inhibitory synaptic connections enable precisely-synchronized irregular firing in IS cells.
source: They connect specifically to each other by gap junctions and mutually inhibitory synaptic connections, which together enable precisely-synchronized irregular firing (Galarreta et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and supported by modeling in Figure 7.

claim: IS cells have wide axonal arborizations through many layers of the cortex.
source: Their wide axonal arborizations through many layers of the cortex and inhibition of pyramidal cells (Galarreta et al., 2004, 2008) suggest that they could exert a powerful influence on the network.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: IS cells inhibit pyramidal cells.
source: Their wide axonal arborizations through many layers of the cortex and inhibition of pyramidal cells (Galarreta et al., 2004, 2008) suggest that they could exert a powerful influence on the network.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: IS cells could exert a powerful influence on the cortical network.
source: Their wide axonal arborizations through many layers of the cortex and inhibition of pyramidal cells (Galarreta et al., 2004, 2008) suggest that they could exert a powerful influence on the network.
evidence: This is an inference based on their anatomical and physiological properties.

claim: IS cells express CB1 cannabinoid receptors.
source: Another distinctive property of these cells is their expression of CB1 cannabinoid receptors, which can suppress their inhibitory output to pyramidal cells, following depolarization of the postsynaptic cell (Galarreta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: CB1 cannabinoid receptors can suppress the inhibitory output of IS cells to pyramidal cells, following depolarization of the postsynaptic cell.
source: Another distinctive property of these cells is their expression of CB1 cannabinoid receptors, which can suppress their inhibitory output to pyramidal cells, following depolarization of the postsynaptic cell (Galarreta et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature on the functional properties of CB1 receptors in these cells.

claim: IS cells make up a large proportion of inhibitory interneurons in superficial layers.
source: Although they make up a large proportion of inhibitory interneurons in superficial layers, they have received much less attention than other classes of interneuron, such as FS and LTS cells.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the relative abundance of IS cells.

claim: IS cells have received much less attention than other classes of interneuron, such as FS and LTS cells.
source: Although they make up a large proportion of inhibitory interneurons in superficial layers, they have received much less attention than other classes of interneuron, such as FS and LTS cells.
evidence: This is stated as background to justify the study.

claim: In the cortex of Gad2-GFP mice, fluorescent cell bodies are concentrated in layer 2.
source: In the cortex of Gad2-GFP mice, fluorescent cell bodies are concentrated in layer 2, with dendrites concentrated in layers 1 and 2/3 and axons which ramify through the cortical layers (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In Gad2-GFP mice, dendrites of fluorescent neurons are concentrated in layers 1 and 2/3.
source: In the cortex of Gad2-GFP mice, fluorescent cell bodies are concentrated in layer 2, with dendrites concentrated in layers 1 and 2/3 and axons which ramify through the cortical layers (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Axons of fluorescent neurons in Gad2-GFP mice ramify through the cortical layers.
source: In the cortex of Gad2-GFP mice, fluorescent cell bodies are concentrated in layer 2, with dendrites concentrated in layers 1 and 2/3 and axons which ramify through the cortical layers (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The morphology of fluorescent neurons in Gad2-GFP mice was varied, with bitufted, bipolar and multipolar cells observed.
source: The morphology of fluorescent neurons was varied, with bitufted, bipolar and multipolar cells observed, as described by Galarreta et al. (2004).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and consistent with previous literature.

claim: IS cells had input resistances of 331 ± 164 MΩ.
source: Cells had input resistances of 331 ± 164 MΩ and passive time constants of 15.4 ± 7.7 ms (mean ± SD, n = 82).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: IS cells had passive time constants of 15.4 ± 7.7 ms.
source: Cells had input resistances of 331 ± 164 MΩ and passive time constants of 15.4 ± 7.7 ms (mean ± SD, n = 82).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: 77% (82/106) of GFP+ cells showed a characteristic pattern of action potentials at irregular intervals in response to a step current stimulus.
source: In response to a step current stimulus in a whole-cell current-clamp recording, 77% (82/106) of the cells showed a characteristic pattern of action potentials (APs) at irregular intervals, with fairly deep and slow afterhyperpolarizations, often following an initial adaptation phase (Figure 1bi).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: IS neurons displayed fairly deep and slow afterhyperpolarizations.
source: In response to a step current stimulus in a whole-cell current-clamp recording, 77% (82/106) of the cells showed a characteristic pattern of action potentials (APs) at irregular intervals, with fairly deep and slow afterhyperpolarizations, often following an initial adaptation phase (Figure 1bi).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental traces shown in Figure 1b.

claim: IS neurons often show an initial adaptation phase in their firing pattern.
source: In response to a step current stimulus in a whole-cell current-clamp recording, 77% (82/106) of the cells showed a characteristic pattern of action potentials (APs) at irregular intervals, with fairly deep and slow afterhyperpolarizations, often following an initial adaptation phase (Figure 1bi).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental traces shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Irregular spiking interneurons displayed larger somata (≈15 µm diameter) than the remaining 23% of GFP+ neurons.
source: Irregular spiking interneurons displayed larger somata (≈15 µm diameter) and more prominent projections than did the remaining 23% of GFP+ neurons, which had a regular-spiking response (excluded from analysis, except when stated), as described by Galarreta et al. (2004, 2008).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Irregular spiking interneurons displayed more prominent projections than regular-spiking GFP+ neurons.
source: Irregular spiking interneurons displayed larger somata (≈15 µm diameter) and more prominent projections than did the remaining 23% of GFP+ neurons, which had a regular-spiking response (excluded from analysis, except when stated), as described by Galarreta et al. (2004, 2008).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: 23% of GFP+ neurons had a regular-spiking response.
source: Irregular spiking interneurons displayed larger somata (≈15 µm diameter) and more prominent projections than did the remaining 23% of GFP+ neurons, which had a regular-spiking response (excluded from analysis, except when stated), as described by Galarreta et al. (2004, 2008).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: The irregular trajectory of action potential intervals in IS neurons varied from trial to trial.
source: The irregular trajectory of action potential intervals in IS neurons varied from trial to trial (Figure 1bii), and the membrane potential showed quite large, variable fluctuations between spikes (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1b and 1c.

claim: The membrane potential of IS neurons showed quite large, variable fluctuations between spikes.
source: The irregular trajectory of action potential intervals in IS neurons varied from trial to trial (Figure 1bii), and the membrane potential showed quite large, variable fluctuations between spikes (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Over long periods of continuous stimulation, the distribution of interspike intervals in IS neurons was skewed and unimodal.
source: Over long periods of continuous stimulation, the distribution of interspike intervals was skewed and unimodal, and could be reasonably well-fitted by a gamma function (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The distribution of interspike intervals in IS neurons could be reasonably well-fitted by a gamma function.
source: Over long periods of continuous stimulation, the distribution of interspike intervals was skewed and unimodal, and could be reasonably well-fitted by a gamma function (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1dii showing the fit.

claim: CV(ISI) was reduced at higher stimulus levels and firing frequencies in IS neurons.
source: CV(ISI) was reduced at higher stimulus levels and firing frequencies, and was quite variable from cell to cell, but ranged from 0.1 (fairly regular) to 0.6 at a firing frequency of ≈10 Hz (CV10 Hz = 0.28 ± 0.15, n = 45).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: CV(ISI) was quite variable from cell to cell in IS neurons.
source: CV(ISI) was reduced at higher stimulus levels and firing frequencies, and was quite variable from cell to cell, but ranged from 0.1 (fairly regular) to 0.6 at a firing frequency of ≈10 Hz (CV10 Hz = 0.28 ± 0.15, n = 45).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: CV(ISI) ranged from 0.1 to 0.6 at a firing frequency of ≈10 Hz in IS neurons.
source: CV(ISI) was reduced at higher stimulus levels and firing frequencies, and was quite variable from cell to cell, but ranged from 0.1 (fairly regular) to 0.6 at a firing frequency of ≈10 Hz (CV10 Hz = 0.28 ± 0.15, n = 45).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The irregularity of IS neurons persisted in the presence of blockers of ionotropic glutamate and GABAA receptors.
source: The irregularity persisted in the presence of blockers of ionotropic glutamate and GABAA receptors and is therefore presumably generated intrinsically, rather than by noisy synaptic input.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation demonstrating the intrinsic nature of irregularity.

claim: The irregularity of IS neurons is presumably generated intrinsically, rather than by noisy synaptic input.
source: The irregularity persisted in the presence of blockers of ionotropic glutamate and GABAA receptors and is therefore presumably generated intrinsically, rather than by noisy synaptic input.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of irregularity in the presence of synaptic blockers.

claim: The intrinsic nature of IS was confirmed in primary cultures of dissociated Gad2 neurons.
source: The intrinsic nature of the IS was confirmed in primary cultures of dissociated Gad2 neurons, which displayed a similar spiking pattern, despite simpler morphology and reduced connectivity (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1e,f showing irregular spiking in cultured neurons.

claim: Primary cultures of dissociated Gad2 neurons displayed a similar irregular spiking pattern, despite simpler morphology and reduced connectivity.
source: The intrinsic nature of the IS was confirmed in primary cultures of dissociated Gad2 neurons, which displayed a similar spiking pattern, despite simpler morphology and reduced connectivity (Figure 1e,f).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1e,f.

claim: Return maps of interspike intervals in IS neurons displayed no discernible fine structure.
source: To characterize the dynamics of irregular spiking, we first examined return maps of interspike intervals – scatter plots of each interval against its predecessor – which displayed no discernible fine structure (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: In five of ten IS cells, both recurrence and determinism were significant (p<0.05).
source: Using a standard sequence size or embedding dimension m = 4, and a neighborhood size (ε) of one standard deviation of the ISIs, we found that in five of ten cells, both recurrence and determinism were significant (p<0.05, z-test), while only recurrence was significant in a further two cells, and in the three remaining cells, neither recurrence nor determinism were significant.
evidence: This is a direct result from the recurrence plot analysis of experimental data.

claim: In two of ten IS cells, only recurrence was significant.
source: Using a standard sequence size or embedding dimension m = 4, and a neighborhood size (ε) of one standard deviation of the ISIs, we found that in five of ten cells, both recurrence and determinism were significant (p<0.05, z-test), while only recurrence was significant in a further two cells, and in the three remaining cells, neither recurrence nor determinism were significant.
evidence: This is a direct result from the recurrence plot analysis of experimental data.

claim: In three of ten IS cells, neither recurrence nor determinism were significant.
source: Using a standard sequence size or embedding dimension m = 4, and a neighborhood size (ε) of one standard deviation of the ISIs, we found that in five of ten cells, both recurrence and determinism were significant (p<0.05, z-test), while only recurrence was significant in a further two cells, and in the three remaining cells, neither recurrence nor determinism were significant.
evidence: This is a direct result from the recurrence plot analysis of experimental data.

claim: Irregular sequences of spikes generated during a constant stimulus in about half of IS neurons show recurrent, correlated sequences of four or more successive intervals.
source: Thus, irregular sequences of spikes generated during a constant stimulus in about half of IS neurons show recurrent, correlated sequences of four or more successive intervals.
evidence: This is concluded from the recurrence plot analysis showing significant recurrence and determinism in 5 of 10 cells.

claim: The concerted action of voltage-dependent ion channel populations would be involved in producing determinism in IS neuron spike trains.
source: It seems likely that the concerted action of voltage-dependent ion channel populations would be involved in producing such determinism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed determinism and the known role of voltage-dependent channels.

claim: Similar recurrence and determinism were found in a conductance-based biophysical model of IS cells.
source: We found similar recurrence and determinism in a conductance-based biophysical model of these cells, described below, when applying the same analysis procedure to its spike trains (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing recurrence plots from the model.

claim: Cells that failed to show significant recurrence and determinism had particularly strong voltage noise in their interspike intervals.
source: We noted that those cells that failed to show significant recurrence and determinism had particularly strong voltage noise in their interspike intervals (not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Membrane potential fluctuations in IS neurons switch on above −50 mV.
source: Clearly, one potentially relevant phenomenon is the noisy fluctuation in the membrane potential which switches on above −50 mV (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Membrane potential fluctuations in IS neurons depend on voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: We found that these fluctuations depended on voltage-gated sodium channels, since they were eliminated by applying tetrodotoxin (TTX; Figure 3b, n = 6 cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3b showing elimination of fluctuations by TTX.

claim: Membrane potential fluctuations in IS neurons were eliminated by applying tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: We found that these fluctuations depended on voltage-gated sodium channels, since they were eliminated by applying tetrodotoxin (TTX; Figure 3b, n = 6 cells).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Cell-attached recordings in somatic patches of IS neurons showed characteristic ≈20 pS inward openings.
source: To further investigate the unitary properties of voltage-gated sodium channels, we carried out cell-attached recordings in somatic patches. Characteristic ≈20 pS inward openings were observed, concentrated soon after the beginning of the depolarization (Figure 3c), with an extrapolated reversal potential of about +120 mV positive to the resting potential, as expected for single voltage-gated sodium channels (Sigworth and Neher, 1980).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Single voltage-gated sodium channels in IS neurons had an extrapolated reversal potential of about +120 mV positive to the resting potential.
source: Characteristic ≈20 pS inward openings were observed, concentrated soon after the beginning of the depolarization (Figure 3c), with an extrapolated reversal potential of about +120 mV positive to the resting potential, as expected for single voltage-gated sodium channels (Sigworth and Neher, 1980).
evidence: This is measured from the experimental data and consistent with known properties of sodium channels.

claim: Frequent late openings of sodium channels were observed up to 100 ms following +40 mV depolarizations from rest in IS neurons.
source: We also observed frequent late openings of the same channel amplitude, up to 100 ms following +40 mV depolarizations from rest, (Figure 3c and d, in 4 out of 5 patches containing transient Na channels).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Whole-cell recordings confirmed the presence of a non-inactivating, TTX sensitive inward current in IS neurons.
source: Whole-cell recordings further confirmed the presence of a non-inactivating, TTX sensitive inward current, evoked in response to a slowly depolarizing ramp (Figure 3e, prominent in 11/13 cells), when K+ and Ca2+ currents were reduced with TEA (2 mM), 4-AP (2 mM) and Cd2+ (200 μM).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: A non-inactivating, TTX sensitive inward current was prominent in 11/13 IS cells.
source: Whole-cell recordings further confirmed the presence of a non-inactivating, TTX sensitive inward current, evoked in response to a slowly depolarizing ramp (Figure 3e, prominent in 11/13 cells), when K+ and Ca2+ currents were reduced with TEA (2 mM), 4-AP (2 mM) and Cd2+ (200 μM).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Stochastic, voltage-dependent gating of sodium channels could be involved in generating irregularity of firing in IS neurons.
source: Thus, stochastic, voltage-dependent gating of sodium channels could be involved in generating irregularity of firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations of persistent sodium channel openings and their voltage dependence.

claim: Sodium-channel-driven subthreshold noise has been observed in other cell types.
source: Sodium-channel-driven subthreshold noise has been observed in other cell types (White et al., 1998), but without appearing to produce the high level of firing irregularity observed in IS cells at ≈10 Hz firing frequencies (Alonso and Klink, 1993).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature to provide context.

claim: The deterministic recurrence of interspike intervals suggests that another active mechanism might be involved in addition to sodium channel noise.
source: The deterministic recurrence of the interspike intervals suggests that another active mechanism might also be involved.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of significant determinism in the recurrence analysis.

claim: Neither blockers of calcium-activated potassium channels nor intracellular perfusion of a fast calcium buffer diminished irregularity of firing in IS neurons.
source: However, neither blockers of calcium-activated potassium channels (iberiotoxin and apamin) nor intracellular perfusion of a fast calcium buffer (BAPTA) diminished irregularity of firing (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and we concluded that intracellular calcium signaling is not centrally involved in the dynamics of intrinsic irregularity.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing no reduction in irregularity with BAPTA.

claim: Intracellular calcium signaling is not centrally involved in the dynamics of intrinsic irregularity in IS neurons.
source: However, neither blockers of calcium-activated potassium channels (iberiotoxin and apamin) nor intracellular perfusion of a fast calcium buffer (BAPTA) diminished irregularity of firing (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and we concluded that intracellular calcium signaling is not centrally involved in the dynamics of intrinsic irregularity.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results showing no effect of calcium buffering on irregularity.

claim: Whole-cell voltage-clamp of IS neurons revealed an early transient outward or A-type potassium current.
source: Whole-cell voltage-clamp of the outward currents in response to families of step depolarizations revealed an early transient outward or A-type potassium current (Figure 4a), which could be isolated by applying a pre-pulse protocol (Amarillo et al., 2008, Maffie et al., 2013) in the presence of 5 mM TEA to remove slower K+ currents (Figure 4b, n = 9).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4a and 4b.

claim: The transient potassium current in IS neurons could be isolated by applying a pre-pulse protocol in the presence of 5 mM TEA.
source: Whole-cell voltage-clamp of the outward currents in response to families of step depolarizations revealed an early transient outward or A-type potassium current (Figure 4a), which could be isolated by applying a pre-pulse protocol (Amarillo et al., 2008, Maffie et al., 2013) in the presence of 5 mM TEA to remove slower K+ currents (Figure 4b, n = 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4b showing the isolated transient current.

claim: Activation and inactivation curves of the transient potassium conductance (gKt) overlapped around the threshold in IS neurons.
source: Fits of the voltage-dependence of the peak conductance and of the steady-state inactivation of this transient potassium conductance (gKt) showed that activation and inactivation curves overlapped around the threshold (Figure 4c, n = 18 cells for inactivation, n = 36 cells for activation), peaking within 1–2 ms, and inactivating over about 20–30 ms (Figure 4d, top).
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The transient potassium current in IS neurons peaked within 1–2 ms.
source: Fits of the voltage-dependence of the peak conductance and of the steady-state inactivation of this transient potassium conductance (gKt) showed that activation and inactivation curves overlapped around the threshold (Figure 4c, n = 18 cells for inactivation, n = 36 cells for activation), peaking within 1–2 ms, and inactivating over about 20–30 ms (Figure 4d, top).
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The transient potassium current in IS neurons inactivated over about 20–30 ms.
source: Fits of the voltage-dependence of the peak conductance and of the steady-state inactivation of this transient potassium conductance (gKt) showed that activation and inactivation curves overlapped around the threshold (Figure 4c, n = 18 cells for inactivation, n = 36 cells for activation), peaking within 1–2 ms, and inactivating over about 20–30 ms (Figure 4d, top).
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The fast inactivating outward current in IS neurons recovered from inactivation with a time constant of around 40 ms at −70 mV.
source: Additionally, this fast inactivating outward current recovered from inactivation with a time constant of around 40 ms at −70 mV (Figure 4d, bottom).
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The properties of the transient potassium current in IS neurons are not consistent with Kv1 channels.
source: These properties are not consistent with Kv1 channels (the current was insensitive to 1 μM α-dendrotoxin, n = 4, not shown), including Kv1.4 (recovery from inactivation in the range of milliseconds rather than seconds, see Wickenden et al., 1999), nor with channels from the Kv3 family (transient currents were TEA insensitive, see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is concluded from pharmacological experiments and comparison with known channel properties.

claim: The gating properties of the transient potassium current in IS neurons closely resemble those of Kv4-family voltage-dependent potassium channels in pyramidal neurons.
source: The gating properties closely resemble those of Kv4-family voltage-dependent potassium channels in pyramidal neurons (Birnbaum et al., 2004), and this was further supported by its sensitivity to 4-AP (Figure 4e top, n = 6) and the specific Kv4.2/4.3 blocker phrixotoxin (PhTX; Figure 4e bottom, n = 7), which produced a partial, reversible block of 55% at a concentration of 5 µM.
evidence: This is concluded from comparison with literature and pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Phrixotoxin produced a partial, reversible block of 55% of the transient potassium current at a concentration of 5 µM.
source: The gating properties closely resemble those of Kv4-family voltage-dependent potassium channels in pyramidal neurons (Birnbaum et al., 2004), and this was further supported by its sensitivity to 4-AP (Figure 4e top, n = 6) and the specific Kv4.2/4.3 blocker phrixotoxin (PhTX; Figure 4e bottom, n = 7), which produced a partial, reversible block of 55% at a concentration of 5 µM.
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The peak transient conductance at 0 mV (gmax0) in IS neurons was estimated to be 22.37 ± 14.41 nS.
source: We fitted conventional Hodgkin-Huxley type models to the voltage-step responses of this current (see Materials and methods), and estimated a peak transient conductance at 0 mV (gmax0, see Materials and methods) of 22.37 ± 14.41 nS (n = 8 cells, mean ± SD).
evidence: This is calculated from fits to the experimental data.

claim: The transient potassium current would be expected to delay the rise of membrane potential just before spike initiation.
source: This current would be expected to delay the rise of membrane potential just before spike initiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the known properties of the current and its activation around threshold.

claim: Averaging the waveform of hundreds of action potentials in IS neurons consistently showed the presence of a clear dip or inflection in the rising phase, about 10 ms before the start of the fast upstroke.
source: Although the membrane potential leading into spikes was generally highly fluctuating, averaging the waveform of hundreds of action potential, aligned with the fastest point of the upstroke, consistently showed the presence of a clear dip or inflection in the rising phase, about 10 ms before the start of the fast upstroke (Figure 4f), which we attribute to this current.
evidence: This is directly observed in the averaged data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The dip or inflection in the rising phase of action potentials in IS neurons is attributed to the transient potassium current.
source: Although the membrane potential leading into spikes was generally highly fluctuating, averaging the waveform of hundreds of action potential, aligned with the fastest point of the upstroke, consistently showed the presence of a clear dip or inflection in the rising phase, about 10 ms before the start of the fast upstroke (Figure 4f), which we attribute to this current.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing and properties of the transient potassium current.

claim: There was a high density of single channel currents in some cell-attached patches (n = 7) with similar activation and inactivation properties to the whole-cell transient potassium current.
source: There was also a high density of single channel currents in some cell-attached patches (n = 7) with similar activation and inactivation properties (Figure 4g and h), implying some clustering in the membrane, as previously described for Kv4 channels (Alonso and Widmer, 1997; Jinno et al., 2005).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4g and h.

claim: The clustering of transient potassium channels in the membrane has been previously described for Kv4 channels.
source: There was also a high density of single channel currents in some cell-attached patches (n = 7) with similar activation and inactivation properties (Figure 4g and h), implying some clustering in the membrane, as previously described for Kv4 channels (Alonso and Widmer, 1997; Jinno et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The single channel conductance of the transient potassium channels in IS neurons appeared to be about 10–12 pS.
source: The fast and small-amplitude single channel openings in these recordings were not well-resolved, but appeared to comprise step transitions corresponding to a single channel chord conductance of about 10–12 pS (assuming EK ≈−90 mV).
evidence: This is estimated from the single channel recordings.

claim: The transient potassium conductance recorded at the soma strongly resembles reported descriptions of Kv4-mediated conductance.
source: Thus, overall, the transient potassium conductance recorded at the soma strongly resembles reported descriptions of Kv4-mediated conductance.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined evidence of kinetics, pharmacology, and single channel properties.

claim: Artificial conductance injection of gKt was sufficient to modulate the spiking irregularity of intrinsically irregular Gad2 interneurons.
source: Artificial conductance injection of gKt was sufficient to modulate the spiking irregularity of intrinsically irregular Gad2 interneurons (Figure 5a–c, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5a-c showing changes in irregularity with gKt injection.

claim: Injecting negative gKt caused a striking regularization of firing in IS neurons.
source: When negative gKt was injected, i.e. subtracting from the dynamics of the native conductance in these cells (as shown in Figure 5d for voltage clamp currents), we saw a striking regularization of firing in the range of frequency examined, as well as a reduction in the afterhyperpolarization (AHP) amplitude.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5a and 5d.

claim: Injecting negative gKt caused a reduction in the afterhyperpolarization (AHP) amplitude in IS neurons.
source: When negative gKt was injected, i.e. subtracting from the dynamics of the native conductance in these cells (as shown in Figure 5d for voltage clamp currents), we saw a striking regularization of firing in the range of frequency examined, as well as a reduction in the afterhyperpolarization (AHP) amplitude.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Injecting positive gKt induced an increase in the irregularity of firing in IS neurons.
source: On the other hand, injecting positive gKt induced an increase in the irregularity of firing, accompanied by a more prominent subthreshold membrane potential fluctuation between spikes (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5a and 5c.

claim: Injecting positive gKt was accompanied by a more prominent subthreshold membrane potential fluctuation between spikes in IS neurons.
source: On the other hand, injecting positive gKt induced an increase in the irregularity of firing, accompanied by a more prominent subthreshold membrane potential fluctuation between spikes (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The effect of gKt on CV(ISI) was consistent especially at lower firing frequencies (e.g. 10 Hz).
source: The effect of gKt on CV(ISI) was consistent especially at lower firing frequencies (e.g. 10 Hz, Figure 5e, n = 42 cells), and it was even more evident when the total gKt injected was normalized to the capacitance of each cell, which is proportional to its plasma membrane area (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5e showing the effect at 10 Hz.

claim: The effect of gKt on CV(ISI) was even more evident when the total gKt injected was normalized to the capacitance of each cell.
source: The effect of gKt on CV(ISI) was consistent especially at lower firing frequencies (e.g. 10 Hz, Figure 5e, n = 42 cells), and it was even more evident when the total gKt injected was normalized to the capacitance of each cell, which is proportional to its plasma membrane area (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5f showing a stronger correlation with normalized conductance.

claim: Pharmacological block of gKt by 4-AP or phrixotoxin gave a similar result to negative conductance injection, reducing irregularity of firing.
source: Pharmacological block of gKt by 4-AP or phrixotoxin gave a similar result to negative conductance injection, reducing irregularity of firing (See Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 showing reduced CV(ISI) with drug application.

claim: 4-AP at 200 or 50 µM decreased CV(ISI) by 44% (n = 5) in IS neurons.
source: When 4-AP was locally perfused at 200 or 50 µM, the CVISI decreased by 44% (n = 5), while PhTX 5 µM caused a mean 23% reduction (b, n = 3).
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: PhTX 5 µM caused a mean 23% reduction in CV(ISI) (n = 3) in IS neurons.
source: When 4-AP was locally perfused at 200 or 50 µM, the CVISI decreased by 44% (n = 5), while PhTX 5 µM caused a mean 23% reduction (b, n = 3).
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: A two-compartment conductance-based biophysical model was constructed comprising a somatic compartment with voltage-dependent conductances linked to a passive dendritic compartment.
source: We constructed a conductance-based biophysical model, in which the key gKt and NaP conductances could be modeled either as stochastic or deterministic elements. A two-compartment model was used, comprising a somatic compartment which contained voltage-dependent conductances, linked to a passive dendritic compartment.
evidence: This describes the computational model developed in the study.

claim: The dendritic compartment was included in the model to capture the extended spatial aspect of the cell morphology.
source: The dendritic compartment was included in order to capture, in a simplified way, the extended spatial aspect of the cell morphology.
evidence: This explains the rationale for the two-compartment structure.

claim: The soma of the model included Kv1 and Kv3 voltage-dependent potassium conductances and a sodium conductance.
source: Similar to a widely-used model of fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons (Erisir et al., 1999; Gouwens et al., 2010), the soma included Kv1 and Kv3 voltage-dependent potassium conductances and a sodium conductance.
evidence: This describes the components of the computational model.

claim: A gKt conductance based on voltage-clamp findings and a persistent sodium conductance (NaP) were added to the model.
source: To this, however, was added a gKt conductance based on the voltage-clamp findings above, and a persistent sodium conductance (NaP).
evidence: This describes the key additions to the model specific to IS neurons.

claim: In the deterministic model, interspike intervals were of two types: long, almost stationary pauses, and periods of subthreshold oscillation.
source: In the deterministic model, interspike intervals were of two types: long, almost stationary pauses, and periods of subthreshold oscillation, of unstable and variable amplitude, at a frequency of about 28 Hz (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the model output shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Subthreshold oscillations in the deterministic model had unstable and variable amplitude at a frequency of about 28 Hz.
source: In the deterministic model, interspike intervals were of two types: long, almost stationary pauses, and periods of subthreshold oscillation, of unstable and variable amplitude, at a frequency of about 28 Hz (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the model output shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The set of conductances in the model gives two dynamical mechanisms for generating irregular interspike intervals: variable numbers of circuits of unstable amplitude subthreshold oscillations, and long pauses in a slow region of phase space.
source: Thus, this set of conductances gives two dynamical mechanisms for generating irregular interspike intervals: variable numbers of circuits of unstable amplitude subthreshold oscillations, and long pauses in a slow region of phase space.
evidence: This is concluded from analysis of the model dynamics shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Changing gKt and NaP conductances to a stochastic form somewhat obscures the difference between pauses and subthreshold oscillations in the model.
source: Changing gKt and NaP conductances to a stochastic form somewhat obscures the difference between the pauses and subthreshold oscillations, causing more irregular and variable fluctuations in the subthreshold oscillations (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the model output shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Subthreshold noise amplitude in the model is highly dependent on the stochastic gKt.
source: The subthreshold noise amplitude is highly dependent on the stochastic gKt, since it is greatly reduced if gKt is deterministic (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6d showing reduced noise with deterministic gKt.

claim: Subthreshold noise amplitude in the model is only slightly reduced if NaP is deterministic.
source: It is only slightly reduced if NaP is deterministic, but greatly reduced if all voltage-gated sodium conductance is removed (Figure 6d, 'TTX' - right hand side).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6d showing the effect of deterministic NaP.

claim: Subthreshold noise amplitude in the model is greatly reduced if all voltage-gated sodium conductance is removed.
source: It is only slightly reduced if NaP is deterministic, but greatly reduced if all voltage-gated sodium conductance is removed (Figure 6d, 'TTX' - right hand side).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6d showing the 'TTX' condition.

claim: Subthreshold fluctuations in the model are dominated by gKt-driven stochastic fluctuations which are strongly amplified by the voltage-gated sodium conductance.
source: This implies that subthreshold fluctuations are dominated by gKt-driven stochastic fluctuations which are strongly amplified by the voltage-gated sodium conductance – both are required.
evidence: This is concluded from the model results shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The greater importance of gKt noise over NaP noise is largely due to its much longer correlation time (10 ms versus 1 ms).
source: The greater importance of gKt noise over NaP noise is largely due to its much longer correlation time (10 ms versus 1 ms), which means that gKt noise is much less filtered by the membrane time constant.
evidence: This is explained based on the known filtering properties of the membrane.

claim: Strong subthreshold membrane potential fluctuations in IS neurons appear to be actively-amplified channel noise.
source: Thus, these strong subthreshold membrane potential fluctuations appear to be actively-amplified channel noise, somewhat like noise-driven subthreshold oscillations, as described in entorhinal stellate neurons (Dorval and White, 2005).
evidence: This is concluded from the model results and comparison with similar phenomena in other neurons.

claim: As the amount of gKt in the membrane is increased to 12 nS, a region of structurally-stable variability is created for firing frequencies up to 20–30 Hz in the model.
source: As the amount of gKt in the membrane is increased to 12 nS, a region of structurally-stable variability is created for firing frequencies up to 20–30 Hz, above which frequency the CV(ISI) subsides, as seen in recordings, in both deterministic (Figure 7a) and stochastic (Figure 7b) forms of the model.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7a and 7b showing the dependence of CV(ISI) on gKt and firing frequency.

claim: Above 20–30 Hz firing frequency, CV(ISI) subsides in the model, as seen in recordings.
source: As the amount of gKt in the membrane is increased to 12 nS, a region of structurally-stable variability is created for firing frequencies up to 20–30 Hz, above which frequency the CV(ISI) subsides, as seen in recordings, in both deterministic (Figure 7a) and stochastic (Figure 7b) forms of the model.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 and matches experimental observations.

claim: In the deterministic form of the model, CV(ISI) reaches values of ≈1, much higher than experimentally observed.
source: In the deterministic form of the model, CV(ISI) reaches values of ≈1, much higher than experimentally observed (red region of surface in Figure 7a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the model output shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The addition of noise dilutes the irregularity of the high-CV region to ≈0.3 in the model, as seen experimentally.
source: However, the addition of noise dilutes the irregularity of this high-CV region to ≈0.3 (Figure 7b), as seen experimentally.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7b showing CV values similar to experimental observations.

claim: The stochastic model shows a much more linear firing frequency-current (f-I) characteristic, as observed in actual recordings.
source: The stochastic model shows a much more linear firing frequency-current (f-I) characteristic, as observed in actual recordings – i.e. the dynamic noise linearizes the input-output relation of these neurons.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the model output in Figure 7b with experimental data.

claim: Dynamic noise linearizes the input-output relation of IS neurons.
source: The stochastic model shows a much more linear firing frequency-current (f-I) characteristic, as observed in actual recordings – i.e. the dynamic noise linearizes the input-output relation of these neurons.
evidence: This is concluded from comparison of deterministic and stochastic model outputs.

claim: In simulated gap-junction-coupled networks of IS cells, firing became highly synchronous as gap junction conductance was increased.
source: In a 5-cell network, firing became highly synchronous as gap junction conductance was increased, as seen in the sharp central peak of cross-correlation (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7c showing increased synchrony with coupling.

claim: CV(ISI) was maintained at the same level as for uncoupled cells, even with strong coupling and complete synchrony in simulated networks of IS cells.
source: However, CV(ISI) was maintained at the same level as for uncoupled cells, even with strong coupling and complete synchrony (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7d showing maintained CV(ISI) with increased coupling.

claim: Nonlinearly-amplified fluctuations are cooperative amongst cells and are well-coupled by the current flow through gap junctions.
source: This perhaps non-intuitive result implies that in effect, nonlinearly-amplified fluctuations are cooperative amongst cells and are well-coupled by the current flow through gap junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from the model results showing maintained irregularity with synchrony.

claim: Elevation of gKt (+3.57 nS gmax0) depresses the synchrony of spikes to 10 Hz gGABA rhythm across the range of oscillation amplitudes tested.
source: Figure 8b shows an example of an IS cell subjected to an elevation of gKt (+3.57 nS gmax0). This depresses the synchrony of spikes to the gGABA rhythm (Figure 8bii,iii) across the range of oscillation amplitudes tested.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8b showing reduced synchrony with added gKt.

claim: Subtraction of gKt enhanced synchrony to 10 Hz oscillation over a wide range of oscillation amplitudes.
source: Conversely, subtraction of gKt from another cell (Figure 8c) enhanced synchrony over a wide range of oscillation amplitudes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8c showing increased synchrony with subtracted gKt.

claim: The effects of gKt on synchrony to 10 Hz inputs are not observed for 40 Hz input.
source: These striking effects of gKt on synchrony to 10 Hz inputs are not observed, however, for 40 Hz input (Figure 8d, summary statistics for the whole set of cells at both frequencies are shown in Figure 8e).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8d and 8e showing no effect at 40 Hz.

claim: Modulation of irregularity of IS neurons by the level of gKt determines their ability to synchronize to oscillatory inhibition.
source: Thus modulation of irregularity of IS neurons by the level of gKt (see Figures 5 and 6) appears to determine their ability to synchronize to oscillatory inhibition, and the dynamics of gKt are such that it can counteract 10 Hz but not 40 Hz rhythms.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The dynamics of gKt are such that it can counteract 10 Hz but not 40 Hz rhythms.
source: Thus modulation of irregularity of IS neurons by the level of gKt (see Figures 5 and 6) appears to determine their ability to synchronize to oscillatory inhibition, and the dynamics of gKt are such that it can counteract 10 Hz but not 40 Hz rhythms.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects at different frequencies shown in Figure 8.

claim: Rejection of synchronization in IS neurons results from the intrinsically irregular dynamics at lower frequencies, around 10 Hz.
source: Rejection of synchronization results from the intrinsically irregular dynamics at lower frequencies, around 10 Hz, while resonance with a noise-obscured subthreshold oscillation (whose frequency in the deterministic model is 28 Hz) could contribute to the stronger synchronization at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Resonance with a noise-obscured subthreshold oscillation (whose frequency in the deterministic model is 28 Hz) could contribute to the stronger synchronization at higher frequencies.
source: Rejection of synchronization results from the intrinsically irregular dynamics at lower frequencies, around 10 Hz, while resonance with a noise-obscured subthreshold oscillation (whose frequency in the deterministic model is 28 Hz) could contribute to the stronger synchronization at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is inferred from the model dynamics and experimental observations.

claim: The native gKt of IS cells allows them to resist synchrony to lower network frequencies such as 10 Hz, while complying readily with higher, gamma frequency rhythms.
source: Thus the native gKt of IS cells allows them to resist synchrony to lower network frequencies such as 10 Hz, while complying readily with higher, gamma frequency rhythms.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results shown in Figure 8.

claim: IS cells could have the effect of destabilizing lower frequency network oscillations while helping to stabilize higher-frequency rhythms.
source: This could have the effect of destabilizing lower frequency network oscillations while helping to stabilize higher-frequency rhythms, and help to determine the times of onset and offset of organized gamma-frequency firing in the network.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential synchronization properties at different frequencies.

claim: IS cells could help to determine the times of onset and offset of organized gamma-frequency firing in the network.
source: This could have the effect of destabilizing lower frequency network oscillations while helping to stabilize higher-frequency rhythms, and help to determine the times of onset and offset of organized gamma-frequency firing in the network.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional role of IS cells.

claim: Irregular-spiking VIP interneurons fire at 10–15 Hz in vivo during whisking and non-whisking activities.
source: This finding is especially relevant considering that irregular-spiking VIP interneurons fire at 10–15 Hz in vivo (whisking and non-whisking activities, Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous in vivo studies.

claim: IS cells have been hard to define functionally because of the profusion of types of inhibitory interneuron in the cortex.
source: IS cells have been hard to define functionally, because of the profusion of types of inhibitory interneuron in the cortex, and because irregular-spiking behavior may also arise from fluctuations in synaptic input or membrane integrity during recordings.
evidence: This is stated as background to explain the challenges in studying IS cells.

claim: Irregular-spiking behavior may arise from fluctuations in synaptic input or membrane integrity during recordings.
source: IS cells have been hard to define functionally, because of the profusion of types of inhibitory interneuron in the cortex, and because irregular-spiking behavior may also arise from fluctuations in synaptic input or membrane integrity during recordings.
evidence: This is stated as a confounding factor in identifying IS cells.

claim: IS interneurons originate from the caudal ganglionic eminence relatively late in development (E16).
source: Inducible in vivo genetic fate mapping (Miyoshi and Fishell, 2011; Miyoshi et al., 2010) has been used to show that these IS interneurons originate from the caudal ganglionic eminence relatively late in development (E16), express 5HT3a receptors, VIP and calretinin, and form about 10% of CGE-derived interneurons, which dominate the more superficial layers of cortex and comprise about 30% of all cortical interneurons.
evidence: This is cited from previous developmental studies.

claim: IS interneurons express 5HT3a receptors, VIP and calretinin.
source: Inducible in vivo genetic fate mapping (Miyoshi and Fishell, 2011; Miyoshi et al., 2010) has been used to show that these IS interneurons originate from the caudal ganglionic eminence relatively late in development (E16), express 5HT3a receptors, VIP and calretinin, and form about 10% of CGE-derived interneurons, which dominate the more superficial layers of cortex and comprise about 30% of all cortical interneurons.
evidence: This is cited from previous molecular characterization studies.

claim: IS interneurons form about 10% of CGE-derived interneurons.
source: Inducible in vivo genetic fate mapping (Miyoshi and Fishell, 2011; Miyoshi et al., 2010) has been used to show that these IS interneurons originate from the caudal ganglionic eminence relatively late in development (E16), express 5HT3a receptors, VIP and calretinin, and form about 10% of CGE-derived interneurons, which dominate the more superficial layers of cortex and comprise about 30% of all cortical interneurons.
evidence: This is cited from previous developmental studies.

claim: CGE-derived interneurons dominate the more superficial layers of cortex and comprise about 30% of all cortical interneurons.
source: Inducible in vivo genetic fate mapping (Miyoshi and Fishell, 2011; Miyoshi et al., 2010) has been used to show that these IS interneurons originate from the caudal ganglionic eminence relatively late in development (E16), express 5HT3a receptors, VIP and calretinin, and form about 10% of CGE-derived interneurons, which dominate the more superficial layers of cortex and comprise about 30% of all cortical interneurons.
evidence: This is cited from previous developmental studies.

claim: Within upper layer 2, IS cells may make up a large proportion, perhaps 50%, of interneurons.
source: Within upper layer 2, the lamina in which they are concentrated, IS cells may make up a large proportion, perhaps 50% (López-Bendito et al., 2004), of interneurons.
evidence: This is cited from previous anatomical studies.

claim: Predictability of spike trains of irregular-spiking cortical neurons has been examined in a previous study which concluded that the variability is not a consequence of low-dimensional, effective deterministic processes.
source: Predictability of spike trains of irregular-spiking cortical neurons has been examined in a previous study (Englitz et al., 2008), which concluded that the variability is not a consequence of low-dimensional, effective deterministic processes.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature to contrast with the current findings.

claim: The previous study on predictability did not examine the genetically-defined population of neurons studied in this manuscript.
source: However, that study did not examine the genetically-defined population of neurons studied here.
evidence: This is stated to explain the difference between the current and previous findings.

claim: The fast-inactivating K+ current found in IS cells is likely to be mediated by Kv4 potassium channel subunits.
source: We suggest that the fast-inactivating K+ current that we found in these cells is likely to be mediated by Kv4 potassium channel subunits, for several reasons.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence including kinetics, pharmacology, and molecular expression data.

claim: IS cells in the GFP mouse model express high levels of Kv4.2 (kcnd2) mRNA, higher than in pyramidal cells and seven times higher than in fast-spiking interneurons.
source: IS cells in this same GFP mouse model have been shown to express high levels of Kv4.2 (kcnd2) mRNA, higher than in a population of pyramidal cells and seven times higher than in a population of fast-spiking interneurons (Sugino et al., 2006), but only very low levels of Kv1.4 (kcna4) transcripts.
evidence: This is cited from previous molecular expression studies.

claim: IS cells express only very low levels of Kv1.4 (kcna4) transcripts.
source: IS cells in this same GFP mouse model have been shown to express high levels of Kv4.2 (kcnd2) mRNA, higher than in a population of pyramidal cells and seven times higher than in a population of fast-spiking interneurons (Sugino et al., 2006), but only very low levels of Kv1.4 (kcna4) transcripts.
evidence: This is cited from previous molecular expression studies.

claim: GFP+ cells in dissociated primary cortical cultures showed robust intrinsic irregular firing.
source: Interestingly, we found that GFP+ cells in dissociated primary cortical cultures also showed robust intrinsic irregular firing (Figure 1e), and expressed transient K+ and persistent Na+ currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1e and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: GFP+ cells in dissociated primary cortical cultures expressed transient K+ and persistent Na+ currents.
source: Interestingly, we found that GFP+ cells in dissociated primary cortical cultures also showed robust intrinsic irregular firing (Figure 1e), and expressed transient K+ and persistent Na+ currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Normal morphology and circuit formation in development are not required for the irregularity of IS neurons.
source: This suggests that normal morphology and circuit formation in development are not required for the irregularity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of irregularity in dissociated cultured neurons.

claim: IS neurons have a relatively high mature input resistance (331 MΩ) compared to other types of interneuron.
source: It is possible that the relatively high mature input resistance of IS neurons (331 MΩ), compared to other types of interneuron could directly lead to greater variability, since single-channel voltage noise should be bigger.
evidence: This is stated as a potential contributing factor to irregularity.

claim: When an intense (2 nS) static shunting conductance was injected, irregularity was not reduced in IS neurons.
source: However, we found that when we injected an intense (2 nS) static shunting conductance, reversing at −70 mV, near to the resting potential – effectively greatly reducing input resistance, the action potential is reduced in amplitude, and afterhyperpolarizations and interspike membrane potential fluctuations are strongly diminished, but irregularity is not reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing maintained irregularity with shunting.

claim: Adding the artificial K+ conductance caused increased, not decreased firing variability in IS neurons.
source: Likewise, adding the artificial K+ conductance, which also decreases input resistance, caused increased, not decreased firing variability.
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Irregularity in IS neurons is produced by a more complex dynamical mechanism, driven partially by stochastic channel opening, but also dependent on the nonlinearity of the transient K+ conductance.
source: This indicates that irregularity is produced by a more complex dynamical mechanism, driven partially by stochastic channel opening, but also dependent on the nonlinearity of the transient K+conductance.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined experimental and modeling results.

claim: The model suggests two deterministic active mechanisms for high spike time variability: long 'pause' states and unstable subthreshold oscillations.
source: The model that we have implemented suggests two deterministic active mechanisms for high spike time variability: long 'pause' states, in which the dynamical state is presumably trapped near the 'ghost' of a fixed point, and unstable subthreshold oscillations.
evidence: This is concluded from analysis of the model dynamics shown in Figure 6.

claim: Both deterministic mechanisms exist over a fairly wide range of values of gKt conductance density and stimulus level.
source: Both these mechanisms exist over a fairly wide range of values of gKt conductance density and stimulus level (Figure 7), but depend on the presence of gKt.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 showing the parameter space of irregularity.

claim: The high irregularity and variability of the purely deterministic form of the model is suggestive of deterministic chaos.
source: The high irregularity and variability of the purely deterministic form of the model is suggestive of deterministic chaos, although a rigorous proof of chaos in the model would require for example proof of a positive Lyapunov exponent, and is beyond the scope of this study.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the model behavior.

claim: Significant dynamical noise must be involved to some extent in the irregularity of IS neurons, as a result of the single-channel characteristics of the main voltage-dependent channels involved.
source: At the same time, however, it is clear that significant dynamical noise must be involved to some extent in the irregularity, as a result of the single-channel characteristics of the main voltage-dependent channels involved.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental observations of single-channel activity and the modeling results.

claim: Adding noise in the model leads to ISI distributions very similar to those observed experimentally.
source: Adding noise in the model, which mimics the single-channel activity of these channels around the AP threshold, realistically obscures the regularity of the subthreshold oscillation, and leads to ISI distributions very similar to those observed experimentally (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, panel a).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing similar ISI distributions.

claim: The interaction of both deterministic Hodgkin-Huxley equations and single-channel dynamical noise is needed for an adequate description of irregular spiking.
source: Thus, we believe that the interaction of both elements, the nonlinear deterministic Hodgkin-Huxley equations and the single-channel dynamical noise is needed for an adequate description of irregular spiking.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined modeling results showing the necessity of both components.

claim: Both the deterministic and stochastic components of the model have measurable biophysical parameters.
source: Both the deterministic and stochastic components of the model have measurable biophysical parameters.
evidence: This is stated to emphasize the biophysical basis of the model.

claim: A bifurcation analysis of an FS cell model incorporating different levels of slowly-inactivating potassium current (Id) showed that higher levels of this current can produce 'stuttering' behavior associated with subthreshold oscillations.
source: For example, a bifurcation analysis (Golomb et al., 2007) of an FS cell model, incorporating different levels of slowly-inactivating potassium current (Id, probably corresponding to Kv1 channels) showed that higher levels of this current can produce 'stuttering' behavior associated with subthreshold oscillations, as also seen experimentally in FS neurons (Tateno et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous modeling studies to provide context.

claim: Dispersion of interspike intervals produced by variations in amplitude of subthreshold oscillations of a much higher frequency (100–150 Hz) characterized in spinal motoneurons has been termed 'mixed-mode' oscillation.

claim: Active irregularity is an energetically-favorable way to generate high spike interval irregularity in individual cells.
source: The active irregularity produced by coordinated activation of populations of voltage-dependent channels and their activation-dependent single-channel noise, which we propose, may have at least two important advantages. First, it is an energetically-favorable way to generate high spike interval irregularity in individual cells, while minimizing unnecessary membrane potential fluctuation, because fluctuations switch on sharply just below AP threshold, and their active amplification makes them highly effective at controlling spike timing.
